name: cardigan
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native) in the HttpArena suite; h2o, mongoose (C) and Drogon (C++) rows in the same table
workload: HttpArena baseline profile (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), plus pipelined, HTTP/2 and h2c baseline profiles, on one 64-core machine; cardigan is a Java io_uring HTTP engine using Panama FFI, virtual threads and the Vector API.
compiler_and_flags: cardigan: eclipse-temurin JDK 26, --enable-preview, jdk.incubator.vector, -Xms512m -Xmx2g -XX:MaxInlineSize=150 -XX:FreqInlineSize=600 (HttpArena frameworks/cardigan/Dockerfile). nginx: -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG. Drogon: CMake Release with jemalloc preloaded. h2o: clang Release -march=native, no LTO.
hardware: HttpArena dedicated 64-core machine, containers per entry (README says '64-core dedicated hardware'; CPU model, RAM, NIC and kernel not stated)
tradeoffs: Experimental alpha Java server needing JDK 26 preview features, Panama FFI and the incubating Vector API; io_uring needs seccomp unconfined in containers; JVM heap 512m-2g and warm-up are not part of the throughput figure.
caveats: The Java server does not win everywhere: at baseline-4096 it is behind libreactorng (C, io_uring) 4,377,377 and libioma (C) 4,255,834; at limited-conn-4096 it is level with or just behind nginx (2,613,832 vs 2,626,297); at baseline-h2-256 h2o is ahead (16,106,978 vs 14,467,569) and agensio (C++) is ahead at h2c-256 (15,185,367 vs 15,144,652). Part of the gap to nginx is epoll versus io_uring, not language. The repo README states no benchmark numbers. Results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; competitor rows (nginx, h2o, mongoose, libreactorng, libioma, drogon, cutelyst, hical, agensio) are read from sibling JSON files in the same directory, entries are minimal hand-written handlers (nginx is a custom C handler module), and the baseline-4096 profile mixes GET and POST with query parsing, not static files. CPU model not stated, so not tier A.

name: statico
workload: Synthetic static in-memory HTTP response served to 1024 connections at 1, 2 and 4 server threads, comparing statico runtimes with nginx, HAProxy, Go net/http, fasthttp, Axum and actix-web.
claimed_speedup: requests/s, 1 / 4 threads: statico (tokio) 399,025 / 1,071,433 vs nginx (return) 286,960 / 832,082 (1.39x / 1.29x, derived from page data); statico (monoio) 656,517 / 1,436,420 (2.29x / 1.73x, derived); README text says standard statico is about 40% faster single-threaded.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release (feature flags per runtime); nginx build and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Designed strictly for benchmarking: returns a fixed response from memory, no routing, no logging; Linux-only io_uring runtimes.
caveats: First-party, no CPU model, load generator or nginx configuration published, so tier C. The README's own observations list monoio at 1.36M req/s at four threads while its table gives 1,436,420. Actix-web (798,809) is slower than nginx (832,082) at four threads in the same table, and the README does not say whether nginx used its tuned worker settings.
found_via: WebSearch 'paper performance evaluation HTTP server written in Rust outperforms nginx C requests per second arXiv' returned docs.rs statico pages; repo from crates.io API (repository field)
why_faster: Pre-built responses held in memory, HTTP pipelining, thread-per-core io_uring runtimes (tokio-uring, monoio, glommio, compio) with CPU pinning for glommio and compio (README).

name: swerver
baseline: nginx (OpenResty alpine image with a tuned nginx.conf)
workload: swerver-benchmarks: k6 scenarios against minimal endpoints (/health, /echo, /blob) in Docker with 2 CPUs and 512 MB per container, swerver vs nginx, actix, http-zig and APISIX.
claimed_speedup: GET /health, 100 VUs, 30 s: swerver 147,435 req/s vs nginx 118,061 (1.25x, derived from page data), actix 133,691; no keep-alive connections/s 90,657 vs nginx 19,206 (4.7x); rapid-fire 143,437 vs nginx 125,346; error handling 114,455 vs nginx 80,053; TLS /health h2 161,781 vs nginx 107,741.
compiler_and_flags: swerver: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (swerver README); nginx: openresty/openresty:alpine image, flags not stated
hardware: Docker Desktop on macOS Apple Silicon, 2 CPU cores and 512 MB per container, April 2026 (exact chip not stated)
tradeoffs: Alpha release; library API will change; HTTP/3 first version runs at 16.5K req/s.

Hot endpoints are served from a per-second-refreshed pre-encoded response cache that skips router, middleware and encoder, while nginx answers /echo through content_by_lua and /health with 'return 200'. Docker Desktop macOS VM, seccomp unconfined so io_uring is used. Results are mixed: mixed workload 36,929 vs nginx 36,969 (tie), /echo latency scenario nginx 8,659 vs swerver 8,517, and actix-web is ahead of swerver on TLS throughput (171,726 vs 161,781). Another Zig server (http-zig) is far behind nginx on several rows.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter)
why_faster: io_uring backend plus a pre-encoded response cache for hot endpoints that skips the router, middleware and response encoder (swerver-benchmarks README).

name: bladebench Zig raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk 8 threads, 1000 connections, 10 s: Zig 80,700 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.98x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (2.45x, derived); the page marks Zig '701k write errors (buffer overrun)'.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 and g++ -O2 for C and C++; 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' with no optimize flag (default Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per source banner). Not -O3 and not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison: the Zig server never calls read() before writing, the Zig build uses no optimisation flag while C/C++ use -O2, each server runs a single-threaded accept loop that closes every connection, ports differ, and the Zig run reports 701k write errors. The README itself notes the Zig I/O errors and recommends 'Zig (if tuned)'. CPU, kernel and compiler versions not stated. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the run-to-run and build noise. Treat as a flagged, low-confidence record.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter) returned Synaptechlabs/bladeBench

baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk 8 threads, 1000 connections, 10 s: Rust 49,388 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.21x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (1.50x, derived), ~0 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 and g++ -O2 for C and C++; 'rustc blade_core.rs' with no -O or opt-level flag (default unoptimised build). Not -O3 and not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison: the Rust build has no optimisation flag while C/C++ use -O2, the Rust server binds 127.0.0.1 while the C++ one binds INADDR_ANY, each is a single-threaded accept loop that closes every connection, and the 10 s single-run differences between all four servers are probably dominated by accept/close behaviour and wrk. Compiler versions, CPU and kernel not stated. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the noise level. Flagged, low-confidence record.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter) returned Synaptechlabs/bladeBench

name: fib
baseline: Sogou workflow (C++ HTTP server) and uSockets (C, BoringSSL) in the lesismal go-*-benchmark repositories; nginx (C) in HttpArena
workload: HTTP/1.1 echo, pipelined, TLS 1.3 echo and WebSocket echo benchmarks, 10,000 connections, 1 KiB payload, GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners with 4 vCPUs (2 for server, 2 for client), single run each.
claimed_speedup: HTTP/1.1 echo: fib 194,671 TPS vs workflow (C++) 150,407 (1.29x, derived from page data), memory 32 MB vs 14 MB; WebSocket echo: fib 138,592 vs uws_events 129,363 (1.07x, derived); README says fib is 'level with or close to' C, C++ and Rust servers; TLS 1.3 echo 103,427 vs uSockets 103,972 (tie).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27, CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' (HttpArena Dockerfile); workflow and uSockets build flags not stated.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 runner, 4 vCPUs (CPU model stated only for a different benchmark: AMD EPYC 9V74)
tradeoffs: Event-loop networking library for Go that keeps the net/http handler model; no LICENSE file found in the repo, so reference only; uses far more memory than workflow (32 MB vs 14 MB) and TLS 1.3 pipelining uses 180 MB vs 51 MB for uSockets.
caveats: First-party single runs on noisy shared runners (the README says read differences of a few percent as ties). It loses to axum on HTTP/1 echo (236,244 vs 194,671), to uSockets and fnet/uws on WebSocket and TLS pipelining, and the workflow pipeline row is missing. In HttpArena it is slightly behind nginx at baseline-4096 (3,164,504 vs 3,284,513) but far ahead on h2c (12,891,491 at 256 connections vs nginx 2,456,329), where nginx is the only C server compared.
found_via: HttpArena results listing (fib.json, frameworks/fib/meta.json) led to the lesismal/fib README
why_faster: A few event loops wait for I/O readiness and a shared worker pool does the work, so an idle connection costs no goroutine; pipelined requests are batched (README).
